clinicalPearls: Incomplete development of the foveal pit with persistence of inner retinal layers over the fovea, so the normal foveal reflex and avascular zone are absent
Commonly presents with reduced acuity and congenital nystagmus, sometimes with mild photophobia
OCT is the key investigation, grading the severity of hypoplasia by the extent of persisting inner retinal layers and outer segment lengthening
Frequently associated with albinism, aniridia and PAX6-related disease, but can occur in isolation
Isolated autosomal recessive foveal hypoplasia has been linked to SLC38A8 mutations, whereas PAX6 disruption underlies aniridia-associated forms
Acuity correlates with the grade of hypoplasia and the integrity of the outer retinal layers
Colour vision and full-field electroretinography are typically preserved, helping distinguish it from cone dystrophies
reference.pathophysiology: Foveal hypoplasia reflects arrest of the normal centrifugal migration of inner retinal neurons and the centripetal packing of cone photoreceptors that create the foveal pit and specialised cone mosaic. Genes governing this process, particularly PAX6, and pigment-related pathways in albinism, are critical; when they are disrupted the inner retinal layers fail to withdraw from the fovea and the foveal avascular zone does not form. The immature fovea provides poor central resolution, which impairs the development of steady fixation and drives congenital nystagmus. Because photoreceptor function itself may be relatively intact, electroretinographic responses are often normal.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution macular OCT to grade foveal hypoplasia
Full-field and, where possible, focal electroretinography
Slit-lamp and iris transillumination assessment for albinism or aniridia
Genetic testing including PAX6, SLC38A8 and albinism genes
redFlags: Progressive visual decline suggesting a coexisting retinal dystrophy rather than stable hypoplasia
Associated aniridia mandating monitoring for glaucoma and, in some, screening for WT1-related Wilms tumour risk
Systemic or developmental features suggesting a wider PAX6 or contiguous gene syndrome
Marked photophobia and absent cone responses pointing to achromatopsia
reference.prognosis: Vision is stable but subnormal, generally correlating with the OCT grade; many individuals retain moderate acuity and benefit from refractive correction and low-vision support.
pitfalls: Diagnosing idiopathic congenital nystagmus without OCT and thereby missing the hypoplasia
Assuming poor acuity is fixed and neglecting a treatable refractive error
Confusing preserved ERG with normality and missing an early cone disorder
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Optimise vision with cycloplegic refraction and spectacle or contact-lens correction of refractive error, as there is no cure for the foveal maldevelopment
Provide low-vision aids and educational and visual rehabilitation support tailored to the subnormal acuity
Manage the associated congenital nystagmus and treat photophobia with tinted lenses, considering prisms or nystagmus surgery in selected cases
Detect and treat amblyopia and refractive error early in childhood to maximise acuity
Screen for and manage associated conditions, including glaucoma and cataract in aniridia and the ocular features of albinism
Offer genetic testing of PAX6, SLC38A8 and albinism genes with counselling and family screening
Provide ongoing ophthalmology follow-up to monitor for associated ocular complications
